subtopic_detail: Milky nipple discharge with a modestly raised hormone level in a woman on antipsychotic treatment
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 28 year old woman referred with milky discharge from both nipples for four months and periods that have become infrequent, with the last one nine weeks ago.

She has schizophrenia treated with risperidone 4 mg daily for the past year with good symptom control, and takes no other medication. She has no headache, no visual field disturbance and no galactorrhoea on only one side. Her thyroid function is normal and a pregnancy test is negative. Her prolactin measured on a single unstressed morning sample is 2100 mIU/L. She tells you that her mental state has been the most stable it has ever been and that she is fearful of any change to her treatment.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral expressible milky nipple discharge, breasts otherwise normal with no mass, visual fields full to confrontation, no acromegalic features
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2100 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), urine pregnancy test negative, urea and electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discuss a change of antipsychotic with her treating psychiatrist and review her prolactin afterwards
options.rationale: A prolactin in this range with symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia in a woman on a strongly prolactin raising antipsychotic is best explained by the drug, and the diagnostic and therapeutic step is a supervised switch to a prolactin sparing agent such as aripiprazole or quetiapine with the level rechecked afterwards. The change is negotiated with her psychiatrist because relapse risk is the competing harm and she is currently stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the pituitary fossa before making any change to her medication
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated when the level is very high, when there are mass effect symptoms such as headache or visual field loss, or when the elevation persists after the offending drug is changed. Scanning first exposes her to an investigation whose most likely result is a normal gland. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start cabergoline at low dose and titrate according to prolactin response with monthly measurements
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists antagonise the very receptor blockade that controls her psychosis and can precipitate relapse, so they are used with great caution and only under specialist supervision in this setting. Changing the causative drug is safer and addresses the mechanism directly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Request macroprolactin measurement on the existing sample to identify a biologically inactive complex
options.rationale: Macroprolactin is the right consideration when a raised level is found in a woman with no symptoms, since the complex is biologically inactive. This woman has genuine galactorrhoea and oligomenorrhoea, which indicates that the excess prolactin is biologically active. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Prescribe a combined oral contraceptive pill to restore withdrawal bleeding and protect her bone density
options.rationale: Oestrogen replacement is a legitimate strategy when the causative drug genuinely cannot be changed, since it protects bone and restores cycles. Offering it first accepts the hyperprolactinaemia and its galactorrhoea rather than removing the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Antipsychotic induced hyperprolactinaemia results from blockade of dopamine receptors in the tuberoinfundibular pathway, and risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride raise prolactin far more than aripiprazole, quetiapine or clozapine. Levels are typically modestly elevated, and the practical rule is that concentrations in the range seen here are compatible with drug effect while much higher values, particularly above about 5000 mIU/L, suggest a prolactinoma and warrant pituitary imaging. The consequences of untreated hyperprolactinaemia are galactorrhoea, oligomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea, sexual dysfunction and, through hypo oestrogenism, reduced bone density over time. Management options are a supervised switch to a prolactin sparing antipsychotic, dose reduction, addition of aripiprazole as a partial agonist, or oestrogen replacement if the drug cannot be changed, with dopamine agonists used only cautiously because they may precipitate psychotic relapse. Every step is taken jointly with the treating psychiatrist because relapse of psychosis is the competing harm.
key_points: Risperidone, paliperidone and amisulpride are the strongest prolactin raising agents
Modest elevations fit drug effect; markedly higher levels suggest a prolactinoma
Symptomatic galactorrhoea and oligomenorrhoea indicate biologically active prolactin
Switch to a prolactin sparing agent is preferred over a dopamine agonist
Untreated hypo oestrogenism carries a long term bone density cost
explanation.pearls: Request macroprolactin testing when a raised prolactin is an incidental finding in a woman with normal cycles and no galactorrhoea, because up to a quarter of such results reflect a biologically inactive immunoglobulin bound complex and reporting it prevents an unnecessary pituitary scan and a needless change of effective antipsychotic treatment.

subtopic_detail: Scant or absent menstruation with cyclical pain following instrumentation of the uterus
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 30 year old woman whose periods have become barely a smear on a pad since she had a suction curettage for retained products of conception seven months ago, complicated by endometritis treated with antibiotics.

Before that pregnancy her periods were heavy and lasted five days. She now has cramping lower abdominal pain each month at the time she expects to bleed, but almost nothing appears. She has been trying to conceive for four months without success. A pregnancy test is negative, her follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol are consistent with normal ovarian function, prolactin and thyroid function are normal, and transvaginal ultrasound reports a thin irregular endometrial echo with some bright linear areas within the cavity.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulva, vagina and cervix, uterus anteverted and normal in size, mild suprapubic tenderness, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Follicle stimulating hormone 6.2 IU/L (follicular phase 3-10), oestradiol 310 pmol/L (follicular phase 90-400), prolactin 280 mIU/L (less than 500), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), transvaginal ultrasound showing a thin irregular endometrial echo with bright linear intracavity areas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer directly for in vitro fertilisation given four months of trying to conceive without success
options.rationale: Assisted reproduction cannot succeed while the cavity is obstructed by adhesion, since an embryo requires receptive endometrium to implant. The structural problem is corrected first, and four months of trying would not by itself meet the usual threshold for referral. (Source: RANZCOG: Recurrent miscarriage)

options.text: Refer for hysteroscopy with a view to adhesiolysis and a strategy to prevent adhesions reforming
options.rationale: Loss of menstrual flow with cyclical pain after uterine instrumentation complicated by infection, alongside normal ovarian hormones and a thin irregular cavity echo, indicates intrauterine adhesions, and hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic gold standard and the treatment. Division under direct vision is combined with a measure to keep the walls apart afterwards, because reformation is the principal problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine adhesions)

options.text: Prescribe a three month course of cyclical oestrogen and progestogen and reassess her bleeding pattern
options.rationale: Cyclical hormones cannot generate bleeding from endometrium that has been replaced by fibrous adhesion, and her own oestradiol is already in the normal range. Oestrogen has a role after adhesiolysis to encourage re epithelialisation rather than as a stand alone treatment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine adhesions)

options.text: Arrange repeat pelvic ultrasound in the luteal phase to reassess the thickness of the endometrium
options.rationale: Repeating the same test in a different phase adds little when the cavity already appears irregular with bright intracavity areas and the clinical picture is characteristic. Saline infusion sonohysterography would add more than a plain repeat, but hysteroscopy remains the definitive assessment. (Source: RANZCOG: Intrauterine adhesions)

options.text: Commence a further course of doxycycline and metronidazole to treat persisting chronic endometritis
options.rationale: The infection was treated seven months ago and there is no fever, discharge or cervical excitation to suggest active infection now. Repeat antibiotics do not reverse fibrous adhesion that has already formed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Intrauterine adhesions form when the basal endometrium is damaged, most often by curettage performed on a recently pregnant uterus and particularly when infection complicates the procedure. The clinical hallmark is a change in menstrual pattern to scant flow or amenorrhoea, frequently with cyclical pain as retained blood cannot escape, together with subfertility and recurrent pregnancy loss. Ovarian function is normal, which is why gonadotrophins, oestradiol, prolactin and thyroid function are unremarkable and why cyclical hormone therapy alone fails to restore bleeding. Ultrasound may show a thin or irregular endometrial echo with bright intracavity areas, and saline infusion sonohysterography improves detection, but hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the treatment. Adhesiolysis is combined with a strategy to prevent reformation and with postoperative oestrogen to promote re epithelialisation, and a second look procedure is often planned because recurrence is common in severe disease.
key_points: Curettage on a recently pregnant uterus, especially with infection, is the classic antecedent
Scant flow or amenorrhoea with cyclical pain and normal ovarian hormones is the pattern
Cyclical hormones alone cannot produce bleeding from adhesion replaced endometrium
Hysteroscopy is both the diagnostic standard and the definitive treatment
Adhesion reformation is the main problem, so prevention and second look are planned
explanation.pearls: Prefer medical management or ultrasound guided gentle evacuation over sharp curettage for retained products where the clinical situation allows, because the single most effective way to treat intrauterine adhesions is to avoid creating them, and the risk rises sharply with repeated instrumentation and with concurrent endometritis.

subtopic_detail: Diffusely enlarged tender uterus with heavy painful bleeding in a woman wanting to conceive
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 38 year old woman with periods that have become progressively heavier and more painful over four years, now soaking through protection hourly on the worst two days. She and her partner have been trying to conceive for eight months.

She describes deep pelvic pressure and pain that begins several days before bleeding starts and continues throughout. On bimanual examination the uterus is diffusely enlarged to about the size of a ten week pregnancy, globular, softer than expected and tender to palpation, with no separate palpable lump and no nodularity in the pouch of Douglas. Transvaginal ultrasound reports asymmetrical myometrial thickening with the posterior wall measuring twice the anterior wall, small myometrial cysts and indistinct borders between the endometrium and the myometrium, and no discrete mass with a surrounding rim.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84/min, BP 114/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Globular tender uterus enlarged to approximately ten week size, no discrete mass, no rectovaginal nodularity, cervix normal, adnexae free
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 104 g/L (115-155), ferritin 8 micrograms/L (30-200), transvaginal ultrasound showing asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts and an indistinct endometrial myometrial junction

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange endometrial ablation to destroy the endometrium and to reduce the volume of menstrual loss
options.rationale: Ablation is contraindicated for any woman who may wish to conceive, and it also performs poorly in adenomyosis because the disease lies deep within the myometrium beyond the reach of the treatment. Pregnancy after ablation carries serious complications. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Prescribe a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist for six months with add back hormone therapy
options.rationale: Ovarian suppression shrinks adenomyotic tissue and controls symptoms effectively but induces a temporary menopause and prevents conception throughout, which is unacceptable to a woman of 38 with declining fertility. It is used before surgery or when other options have failed. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Treat the iron deficiency and offer a non hormonal option for bleeding and pain while she conceives
options.rationale: The ultrasound and examination findings describe adenomyosis, and every hormonal treatment for it works by suppressing ovulation or the endometrium, which is incompatible with her wish to conceive now. Iron replacement corrects the anaemia driving her fatigue, and tranexamic acid with a non steroidal anti inflammatory taken during menstruation reduces both loss and pain without preventing conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel intrauterine device as the most effective treatment for her bleeding and pain
options.rationale: This device is genuinely the most effective medical treatment for the bleeding and pain of adenomyosis, but it is a contraceptive and would prevent the pregnancy she is actively seeking. It becomes the treatment of choice once her family is complete. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation to reduce the uterine volume and to control the heavy bleeding
options.rationale: Embolisation reduces bleeding but carries a risk of diminished ovarian reserve and adverse effects on subsequent pregnancy, so it is not offered to a woman actively seeking conception. It is considered for women who have completed childbearing and wish to avoid hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium and typically presents in the later reproductive years with progressive heavy bleeding, dysmenorrhoea that starts before the flow, and pelvic pressure. Examination shows a diffusely enlarged globular tender uterus, in contrast to the firm irregular asymmetrically enlarged uterus of fibroids, and the ultrasound features are asymmetrical myometrial thickening, myometrial cysts, echogenic subendometrial lines and an indistinct junctional zone without the discrete mass and pseudocapsule of a fibroid. The therapeutic difficulty is that the most effective treatments all suppress ovulation or the endometrium and are therefore unusable in a woman trying to conceive. In that situation the practical plan is to correct iron deficiency and to use tranexamic acid with a non steroidal anti inflammatory during menstruation, both of which reduce loss and pain without preventing conception. Adenomyosis itself is associated with reduced implantation and increased miscarriage, so referral for fertility assessment is reasonable if conception does not occur.
key_points: Globular tender uterus with pain preceding the flow suggests adenomyosis over fibroids
Ultrasound shows asymmetrical thickening and myometrial cysts without a discrete mass
The levonorgestrel device is the most effective medical treatment but is contraceptive
Ablation and embolisation are unsuitable for women seeking future pregnancy
Tranexamic acid and a non steroidal anti inflammatory reduce loss without blocking conception
explanation.pearls: Treat the ferritin of 8 micrograms per litre as a diagnosis in its own right rather than a footnote to the bleeding, because iron deficiency at this level causes fatigue and reduced exercise tolerance well before the haemoglobin falls far, and an intravenous infusion restores stores in a single visit when oral iron is poorly tolerated or when conception is being actively sought.

subtopic_detail: Burning pain reproduced by light touch at the vestibule with normal vulval skin
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar seeing a 24 year old woman with two years of burning pain at the vaginal entrance whenever anything touches it, including tampons, tight jeans and intercourse. She says the pain begins the instant there is contact and lasts for hours afterwards.

She has been treated with four courses of topical and oral antifungals over the past year, each prescribed for presumed thrush, without any benefit. She has no discharge, no itch and no odour. On examination the vulval skin is entirely normal with no erythema, no fissuring, no pallor, no loss of architecture and no lesions. Light contact with a cotton bud at the posterior vestibule reproduces her pain sharply and reproducibly, while the same touch on the labia majora and the inner thigh causes nothing. A high vaginal swab and culture taken last month were negative.

data_table.Examination: Normal vulval architecture and colour, no fissures, erosions or lesions, cotton bud testing sharply positive at the posterior vestibule and negative on labia majora and thigh, pelvic floor muscles tender and hypertonic on gentle digital assessment
data_table.Investigations: High vaginal swab with fungal culture negative, no other tests performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Perform a vulval punch biopsy of the vestibule to establish the histological diagnosis before treatment
options.rationale: Biopsy is indicated when the skin looks abnormal, when a dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus or lichen planus is suspected, or when malignancy must be excluded. Normal skin with a purely sensory abnormality yields nothing on histology and adds a painful procedure. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvar pain)

options.text: Refer for vestibulectomy to excise the painful tissue as the definitive surgical treatment of her pain
options.rationale: Vestibulectomy has reasonable success rates but is reserved for women with localised provoked pain who have failed conservative treatment including physiotherapy and medical therapy. Operating before those measures have been tried is not justified in a woman of 24. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvar pain)

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid ointment nightly for three months to settle vulval inflammation
options.rationale: Potent topical corticosteroid is the treatment for an inflammatory vulval dermatosis such as lichen sclerosus, recognised by pallor, fissuring and loss of architecture. Prolonged application to normal skin causes atrophy without treating a neuropathic pain process. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatology)

options.text: Stop all antifungal treatment and refer for pelvic floor physiotherapy with psychosexual support alongside
options.rationale: Reproducible burning provoked by light touch confined to the vestibule with entirely normal skin is localised provoked vulvodynia, a pain disorder rather than an infection, and repeated antifungals maintain an irritant contact dermatitis that worsens it. Pelvic floor physiotherapy addressing the associated muscle hypertonicity, combined with psychological and sexual therapy, has the strongest evidence base in this condition. (Source: RANZCOG: Vulvar pain)

options.text: Prescribe a six month course of weekly oral fluconazole for chronic recurrent vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.rationale: Suppressive antifungal therapy is appropriate for culture confirmed recurrent candidiasis, which presents with itch and discharge and responds at least partially to treatment. Negative cultures and four failed courses point away from a fungal cause entirely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Vulvodynia is vulval pain of at least three months duration without an identifiable cause on examination, and the commonest form is localised provoked pain at the vestibule, in which light touch produces sharp burning that outlasts the stimulus. The cotton bud test is the central examination finding, reproducing pain at the vestibule while adjacent skin is unaffected, and the skin itself must be normal for the diagnosis to be made. Coexisting pelvic floor muscle hypertonicity is very common and is a major contributor to the pain cycle. The most frequent clinical error is repeated empirical antifungal treatment, which not only fails but produces an irritant dermatitis that amplifies the symptom. Management is multimodal, with pelvic floor physiotherapy and psychosexual therapy as the core, topical local anaesthetic and vulval care measures as adjuncts, neuromodulator medication for some, and vestibulectomy reserved for refractory localised disease.
key_points: Normal skin with reproducible vestibular pain on cotton bud testing defines the condition
Repeated empirical antifungals fail and cause irritant dermatitis that worsens pain
Pelvic floor hypertonicity is a common and treatable contributor
Physiotherapy with psychosexual therapy has the strongest evidence base
Biopsy and surgery are for abnormal skin and for refractory disease respectively
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically whether the pain is provoked only by contact or is also present unprovoked while sitting or resting, because unprovoked generalised vulvodynia responds better to neuromodulator medication such as amitriptyline or a gabapentinoid, while the provoked localised form responds best to physiotherapy and local measures, and the two are frequently managed as if they were one condition.

subtopic_detail: Sudden severe unilateral pain in early pregnancy after ovarian stimulation with enlarged ovaries
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar called to the emergency department at 2 am to see a 32 year old woman at 6 weeks gestation after a single embryo transfer, her fourth cycle of treatment and her first pregnancy.

She woke four hours ago with sudden severe right sided pain that comes in waves, and has vomited five times. She was reviewed three days ago for abdominal distension and was told her ovaries were enlarged from the stimulation. Transvaginal ultrasound now shows an intrauterine gestational sac with a foetal pole and cardiac activity, a right ovary measuring 82 mm with multiple peripherally displaced follicles and stromal oedema, a left ovary measuring 74 mm, moderate free fluid, and preserved arterial flow with absent venous flow in the right ovary. Her haemoglobin is 158 g/L with a haematocrit of 0.48 and her albumin is 29 g/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 116/min, BP 104/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen with shifting dullness, severe right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, cervix closed, no vaginal bleeding, urine output 20 mL in the last two hours
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 158 g/L (115-155), haematocrit 0.48 (0.35-0.45), white cell count 16.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), creatinine 92 micromol/L (45-90), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), transvaginal ultrasound showing viable intrauterine pregnancy, right ovary 82 mm with peripheral follicles and stromal oedema, absent venous flow with preserved arterial flow on the right, moderate ascites

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Admit for intravenous fluid, analgesia and serial review, deferring surgery while the pregnancy is early
options.rationale: Conservative management is correct for the pain of hyperstimulation without torsion, but a twisted ovary infarcts within hours and delay converts a salvageable organ into a necrotic one. Early pregnancy is not a reason to withhold laparoscopy, which is safe in the first trimester. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Proceed to laparoscopy and perform right salpingo oophorectomy because a torted ovary is not salvageable
options.rationale: Removing the adnexa was historical practice based on fear of releasing thromboembolism, which evidence has not supported, and function recovers in most ovaries that look black at the time of untwisting. Oophorectomy in a woman with a hard won pregnancy and possible future cycles destroys reserve unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Perform ultrasound guided paracentesis of the ascites to relieve pressure and improve her urine output
options.rationale: Drainage of ascites genuinely relieves severe hyperstimulation and improves renal perfusion and respiratory function, and she will likely need it. It does nothing for a twisted pedicle and treating only the hyperstimulation would leave the torsion to progress to infarction. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Arrange urgent magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to confirm the diagnosis before operative treatment
options.rationale: Magnetic resonance imaging is safe in pregnancy and can demonstrate torsion, but arranging it overnight introduces a delay of hours in a time critical ischaemic process. The diagnosis here is clinical and the operation is both confirmatory and therapeutic. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

options.text: Resuscitate with intravenous fluid and proceed to laparoscopic detorsion with conservation of the ovary
options.rationale: Absent venous flow with preserved arterial flow in a massively enlarged stimulated ovary alongside sudden severe pain and vomiting is torsion, and preserved arterial signal never excludes it because the dual blood supply and the sequence of venous then arterial occlusion make Doppler unreliable. Untwisting rather than removing the adnexa preserves ovarian function and is safe even when the ovary looks dusky, while the intravascular depletion from hyperstimulation is corrected before and during anaesthesia. (Source: RANZCOG: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome)

explanation.summary: Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome and ovarian torsion are linked because stimulated ovaries become heavy and mobile, and torsion complicates a meaningful minority of moderate to severe cases, with the risk rising further once pregnancy occurs and human chorionic gonadotrophin sustains the enlargement. The diagnostic trap is Doppler: the ovary has a dual arterial supply and venous flow is lost before arterial flow, so preserved arterial signal is common in confirmed torsion and must never be used to exclude it. This patient simultaneously has severe hyperstimulation, evidenced by haemoconcentration, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites, oliguria and rising creatinine, which raises anaesthetic and thromboembolic risk and requires fluid resuscitation and thromboprophylaxis planning around the operation rather than instead of it. Management is prompt laparoscopic detorsion with conservation, since even a black ovary recovers function in the great majority and oophorectomy is rarely justified. Ongoing care includes continued management of the hyperstimulation, which will persist and may worsen for days as the pregnancy advances.
key_points: Preserved arterial Doppler flow does not exclude ovarian torsion
Pregnancy after assisted reproduction prolongs and worsens hyperstimulation
Haemoconcentration, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites and oliguria mark severe hyperstimulation
Detorsion with conservation is preferred; a dusky ovary usually recovers function
Resuscitate and plan thromboprophylaxis around the operation rather than delaying it
explanation.pearls: Prescribe thromboprophylaxis with low molecular weight heparin and graduated compression around the operation, because severe hyperstimulation combines haemoconcentration, immobility, pregnancy and an operative insult, and the thrombotic events that characterise this syndrome occur in unusual sites such as the internal jugular and subclavian veins and can present weeks after the ovaries have settled.
